rows.l1_text: In recent years, many countries have begun to limit the use of single-use plastic products through legislation, and this is part of a global trend.
The goal of these environmental policies is to reduce plastic pollution and protect natural resources.
Different countries have adopted different regulatory methods.
Some countries forbid supermarkets from providing plastic bags for free, and people need to pay to buy them, which can reduce the amount used.
Other countries completely ban certain plastic products, such as plastic straws and tableware.
The government will also tax companies that make plastic, encouraging them to switch to environmentally friendly materials.
In Europe, some countries have introduced a "plastic bottle deposit system".
When customers buy drinks, they pay a little extra, and after returning the empty bottle they can get the deposit back.
This method has greatly increased the recycling rate of plastic bottles.
Some cities in Asia, on the other hand, have strengthened waste sorting management, stipulating that residents must put plastic waste out separately, otherwise they will be fined.
Although these measures sometimes bring inconvenience to life, in the long run they are beneficial to the environment.
Although countries' policies differ, their aim is all to reduce plastic waste.
Scientists point out that plastic is very hard to break down in the natural environment and will cause harm to marine life.
Therefore, more and more countries are joining this action.
Experts believe that effective regulation requires the joint effort of the government, businesses and the public.
Only if everyone cooperates can the problem of plastic pollution be truly solved.
This global trend also reminds us that protecting the environment is everyone's responsibility.
In future there may be stricter laws introduced, pushing society to develop in a more sustainable direction.

The recycling symbol is an important symbolic meaning of environmentalism.

It quickly became popular and was used in many countries.
The three arrows of this symbol represent three steps of waste management: reduce use, reuse, and recycle.
The first arrow is reducing the things thrown away, the second is using old things again, and the third is turning garbage into new things.
Although the recycling systems of different countries differ, this symbol helps people understand the importance of protecting the environment.
Today, we can see this symbol on cardboard boxes, plastic bottles and metal cans.
Although the recycling policies in some places are different, this design makes it easier for people all over the world to recognize the meaning of recycling.
Environmentalism is not only the responsibility of the government; everyone can start by sorting garbage.

Making compost at home is a very practical do-it-yourself project that can both reduce waste and provide good fertilizer for gardening.
Many people throw organic waste such as vegetable leaves, fruit peels and coffee grounds from the kitchen into the trash can, but actually these can all become useful compost.
First, prepare a plastic box with a lid and put it on the balcony or in a corner of the yard.
A few small holes must be made in the box bottom, for drainage and air.
Next, in the box, first lay a layer of dry leaves or torn-up paper, and then add kitchen waste.
Each time after adding wet waste, cover it with a layer of dry material, which can reduce the smell and also help decomposition.
Do not put meat, oil and dairy products into the compost box, because they easily attract bugs and are also hard to decompose.
Every one or two weeks, turn the compost with a shovel to let air in, so that the waste will decompose faster.
After about two months, the original waste will turn into something dark brown and like soil, and this is compost.
Mix it into the soil of flowerpots or vegetable gardens, and the plants will grow better.
This process reflects the idea of sustainability, because we are recycling resources instead of treating them as waste.
Making compost yourself is not only environmentally friendly, but also lets people better understand the cycles of nature.
Even a small action can have a positive impact on the environment.

In the development landscape of contemporary metropolises, urban green spaces and vertical farms have gone beyond their purely ecological function and evolved into strategic elements reshaping the economic geography.

Parks, community gardens, and even the greening systems on building facades and rooftops, traditionally regarded as "non-productive spaces", are being deeply embedded in the urban capital cycle through multiple value chains.

The market premium mechanism of high-end real estate projects is significantly driven by landscape resources, and residential units adjacent to or integrating high-quality green space often achieve a value increase of more than 20%, a phenomenon especially prominent in the core areas of first-tier cities where land is scarce.

Investors no longer evaluate only floor area and location, but incorporate the accessibility of "green capital" into core risk assessment models, pushing developers to regard ecological infrastructure as a key lever for improving asset liquidity.
At the same time, vertical farms, as an advanced form of urban agriculture, are reconstructing the spatiotemporal logic of food security.

Through multi-layer hydroponics, aeroponics and artificial intelligence environmental control technology, such facilities can achieve, within a three-dimensional space of tens of thousands of square meters, an output efficiency equivalent to hundreds of hectares of traditional farmland, and supply fresh leafy vegetables and medicinal plants without interruption all year round.
Their characteristic of being located close to end consumers greatly reduces logistics losses and the carbon footprint, forming a resilient alternative to fragile global supply chains.

When frequent extreme weather causes fluctuations in staple grain producing areas, distributed urban food production networks show a significant risk-hedging capacity, leading local governments to include such projects in the emergency planning of critical infrastructure.
Viewed from the macro perspective of urban planning, sustainability has been transformed from a moral initiative into economic rationality.

Mixed-use development is being redefined: a commercial complex integrating a vertical farm is no longer merely a display of corporate social responsibility, but becomes a business strategy for attracting high-end tenants and increasing brand stickiness.

Through policy tools such as floor-area-ratio bonuses and tax reductions, the government guides private investment toward construction projects with ecological service functions, thereby lowering public finance's long-term spending on sewage treatment, heat island mitigation and air pollution control.

This innovative financing model of public-private collaboration has given rise to new financial instruments such as "environmental benefit bonds", which securitize externality benefits such as incremental carbon sinks, energy savings and improved residents' health, opening up a quantifiable return path for sustainable investment.
A more far-reaching impact lies in the re-agendaization of spatial justice.
When green space and localized food production become scarce resources, their mode of distribution is directly linked to social stratification.

Cutting-edge urban governance practices are trying to ensure, through legal mandates and incentive mechanisms, that low-income communities also enjoy technology-enabled agricultural facilities and high-quality green space, avoiding the entrenchment of ecological privilege.

Against this background, the city is no longer seen as the opposite of nature, but, through technological innovation and institutional design, becomes a complex adaptive system in which sustainability, food sovereignty and economic vitality co-evolve.
The foundation of real estate value is shifting from the possession of a single physical space to the dynamic capacity to contribute to ecological service flows and community well-being.

In the precise system of modern aeronautical engineering, the design of aircraft is essentially an artistic application of physical laws, and aerodynamic principles in particular occupy the core position within it.
When an aircraft travels through the atmosphere, the interaction between its wings and the airflow determines the basic feasibility of flight.

The core of this process lies in the mechanism by which lift is generated: the airflow over the upper surface of the wing speeds up because of its greater curvature, causing the pressure to drop; by comparison, the airflow over the lower surface is slower, and the pressure is relatively higher.
This pressure difference is perpendicular to the direction of the airflow and forms a net upward force, namely lift.
According to Bernoulli's theorem, an increase in fluid velocity is necessarily accompanied by a decrease in static pressure, which provides a classical physical explanation for lift.

However, relying only on Bernoulli's principle is not enough to fully describe complex real flow phenomena, so modern aerodynamics tends to combine it with Newton's third law for comprehensive analysis: the wing deflects the airflow downward through the angle of attack, and the airflow in turn pushes the wing upward with an equal and opposite force, thereby producing lift.
During flight, lift is not the only force acting on the aircraft.

Coexisting with it is drag, which is the opposing force that air exerts on the forward motion of the aircraft, and which can be subdivided into many types such as pressure drag, friction drag and induced drag.

Pressure drag arises from the pressure imbalance between the front and rear of the aircraft, and is especially pronounced where the fuselage cross-section changes sharply; friction drag comes from the viscous shear between air molecules and the aircraft surface, and is greatly affected by surface roughness and the Reynolds number; and induced drag is a by-product of lift, caused by the local downwash airflow induced by wingtip vortices, and its strength increases as lift increases.

To achieve efficient cruising, aeronautical engineers must make careful trade-offs in aerodynamic configuration in order to maximize the lift-to-drag ratio, that is, the lift that can be produced per unit of drag, which is a key indicator for measuring flight efficiency.
From the perspective of engineering implementation, aircraft design is an optimization game of multidisciplinary coupling.

Advances in materials science have allowed composite materials to be widely used, which not only reduces structural weight but also enhances fatigue durability; the development of computational fluid dynamics, CFD, enables engineers to simulate aerodynamic performance under extreme operating conditions in virtual wind tunnels, thereby completing multiple rounds of iteration before prototype manufacturing.

In addition, active flow control technologies, such as boundary layer suction or synthetic jets, are being explored for adjusting airflow separation in real time, further extending the flight envelope.

Behind these cutting-edge technologies is the in-depth solution of the Navier-Stokes equations, whose nonlinear nature makes turbulence modeling still a problem that the physics community has not fully conquered to this day.
It is worth noting that even in modern airliners highly integrated with autonomous driving and artificial intelligence, the basic physical laws of aerodynamics still cannot be violated.
All the control actions performed by pilots or flight control systems, whether pitch, roll or yaw, ultimately come down to the precise regulation of aerodynamic moments.

The aerodynamic challenges that an aircraft faces in different flight phases, such as takeoff, cruising and landing, differ, requiring the wing shape, such as the deployment of flaps and slats, to adapt dynamically.
From this it can be seen that aeronautical engineering is not only a collection of technologies, but also an externalized manifestation of humanity's deep understanding of the laws of nature.

Every smooth takeoff and landing is the result of rigorous adherence to the laws of physics, and also demonstrates the outstanding ability of engineering wisdom to achieve controllability in complex systems.

In the practical dimension of contemporary environmental ethics, the household composting system has become a micro-level carrier that embodies the concept of urban sustainability, not only reflecting an individual's active assumption of ecological responsibility, but also constituting an indispensable distributed node in the city's waste reduction strategy.

Through the localized cyclical conversion of organic waste, the household-level resource reuse mechanism effectively shortens the traditional waste treatment chain, thereby lowering the carbon footprint and strengthening community-level ecological resilience.

This DIY-type ecological intervention is essentially a gentle reconstruction of the industrialized consumption model, and behind it lies a deep philosophy of horticulture, namely that a non-exploitative symbiotic relationship should be established between people and the land.
To achieve efficient and hygienic household composting, the first thing is to understand the biochemical balance between "green materials" and "brown materials".

Green materials are rich in nitrogen and include wet organic matter such as kitchen peelings, coffee grounds and fresh grass clippings; brown materials provide a carbon source, such as dry residues like dry leaves, shredded cardboard and sawdust.

The ideal ratio is about 1:2 by volume; this carbon-to-nitrogen ratio can promote the succession from mesophilic to thermophilic microbial communities, raising the pile to 55–65°C within a few days and effectively inactivating pathogens and weed seeds.
Special attention must be paid to strictly excluding animal-derived residues such as meat, fats and dairy products, because they easily cause anaerobic fermentation, breeding odors and pests.
The choice of composting container must suit local conditions.

City apartments can use a sealed vermicomposter, using the gut microbes of red earthworms, Eisenia fetida, to efficiently break down finely chopped kitchen waste, producing a humus concentrate rich in plant growth hormones, the "black gold".

Those with a yard should build a layered composting bin, using physical separation to achieve continuous processing of different fermentation stages: the bottom layer is the primary decomposition zone, the middle layer is the maturation transition zone, and the top layer continuously receives new material.
Regular aerobic turning of the pile ensures oxygen penetration and prevents local anaerobic acidification, and is the key operation for maintaining the activity of the microbial community.
From the perspective of ecological engineering, household composting is in fact a low-entropy cycle model.

Traditional landfilling makes organic matter decompose under anaerobic conditions, releasing methane, CH₄, a potent greenhouse gas, whereas aerobic composting converts it into stable humus, sequestering carbon in the soil matrix.

When this matured product is applied to a household gardening system, it not only improves the soil's aggregate structure and enhances its water and nutrient retention, but also rebuilds the positive feedback loop among plants, microorganisms and organic matter.

Research shows that in planting beds that have long used homemade compost, the microbial diversity index is more than 40% higher than in the control group, significantly enhancing plants' stress resistance.
Especially profound is that this daily practice contains a "cognitive transformation effect" in the sense of behavioral ecology.

When individuals personally experience the complete cycle of a banana peel turning into fertile soil, the boundary of their cognition of the concept of "waste" will fundamentally shift: waste is no longer the end point of linear consumption, but an intermediary of cyclical metabolism.

This kind of embodied cognition then catalyzes broader sustainable lifestyle choices, forming a chain reaction of behavior from waste reduction to low-carbon travel and from organic consumption to energy saving.

Therefore, household composting is not only a technical operation, but also a ritual practice of constructing ecological subjectivity, reshaping the ethical contract between humans and nature within micro-level life politics.

The evolution of the notation system profoundly reflects the historical course of humanity's understanding of the order of sound.
Since ancient times, different civilizations have tried to capture fleeting sounds with visual symbols, but early notation methods were mostly suggestive rather than precise.

Ancient Greece used letters to mark pitch, Byzantium used symbols to indicate the direction of the melody, and Chinese gongche notation used characters to record relative pitch positions; none of these systems specified rhythmic details, and their performance relied on the tradition of oral transmission.

The truly revolutionary turning point began with the development of neume notation in late medieval Western Europe; monks added symbols above scripture texts to indicate the rise and fall of notes, which eventually evolved into the four-line staff, whose foundation was laid by Guido d'Arezzo in the 11th century.
This system achieved a spatial representation of pitch through the clear correspondence between lines and spaces, and provided a necessary condition for the systematization of music theory.
By the Renaissance, the five-line staff was gradually established as the standard, and with the introduction of bar lines, key signatures and time signatures, notation became increasingly precise.
This technical evolution not only allowed the complex texture of polyphonic music to be conveyed accurately, but also profoundly influenced composers' ways of thinking.
When sound can be completely recorded, creation is no longer limited to the scope of improvised performance, but becomes an intellectual activity that can be deliberated over and revised on paper.

In the Baroque era, the popularity of figured bass notation further reflected the maturity of the concept of functional harmony; and from the Classical to the Romantic period, notation increasingly tended toward comprehensive control, with dynamics, tempo and expression markings appearing densely, reflecting the central position of individual emotional expression in music.
Since the 20th century, traditional notation has faced multiple challenges.

Schoenberg's twelve-tone system forced theorists to reconstruct the logic of pitch organization, and serialism brought parameters such as rhythm, duration and dynamics all under control, giving rise to a highly mathematical notational language.

At the same time, avant-garde composers such as John Cage questioned the authority of traditional notation, developing graphic scores, text scores and even the open structures of chance music, emphasizing the performer's right to re-create.

The rise of electronic music brought an entirely new dimension: technical means such as spectrum analysis, waveform diagrams and algorithmically generated scores allowed notation to go beyond the visual paradigm of the staff and enter the field of data-based expression.
Today, the development of notation presents a pattern of pluralistic coexistence.

The traditional five-line staff is still the globally accepted technical language, supporting symphony orchestras, opera productions and academic composition teaching; while in the field of experimental music, mixed-media notation and real-time interactive notation, such as visual instructions in the Max/MSP environment, are constantly expanding the boundaries.

It is worth noting that after artificial intelligence became involved in music creation, machine-generated scores often combine symbolic logic with probabilistic models, prompting new discussions about "readability" and "playability".

Viewed from a historical dimension, notation is not only the evolution of a technical tool, but also a mirror of changes in the concept of the nature of music; it both shaped the way composers imagine, and reconstructed the cultural coding of auditory experience.

The development of notation is, in essence, humanity's perpetual effort to capture infinite sonic possibilities with a finite system of symbols, and its trajectory of evolution is a profound testimony to the interactive symbiosis of music theory and practice.

The history of music is long, and musical notation is also slowly developing.
The earliest music had no fixed way of notation, and people learned by ear.
Later, composers needed to write their music down so that more people could perform it.
So, different notation systems appeared.
In ancient times, some places used letters to represent pitch, and some used symbols.
These methods were simple, but could not accurately record rhythm and duration.
With the progress of music theory, notation became more refined.
An early form of staff notation appeared in medieval Europe.
At first there were only two lines, and later it became five lines, which could show the height of notes more clearly.
This notation was used by many composers and also spread to other regions.
Although different places have different habits, the five-line staff gradually became the internationally accepted method.
In China, ancient times also had their own notation methods, such as gongche notation and jianzi notation.
They use Chinese characters or symbols to record fingering and note positions, and are suitable for traditional instruments.
Although many people today study Western five-line staff notation, these ancient methods still have value.
Studying them can help us understand the history of music.
Modern technology has also brought new ways of notation.
Some composers use graphic scores, drawing music as images.
There are also people who use digital software to edit sound directly.
These new methods make musical creation freer.
Overall, the development of notation reflects humanity's constant pursuit of musical expression.
From simple symbols to complex systems, it helps music cross time and space and be understood and performed by more people.
SaaS companies need to take data and algorithm compliance issues seriously.
When users use a service, they provide a lot of personal information.
Companies must tell users clearly how this data will be used.
For example, the system needs to explain which data is used to improve the product and which might be shared with partners.
If users do not understand the explanation, they cannot make the right choice.
Therefore, the wording must be simple and clear, avoiding words that are too technical.
In addition, how algorithms work should also have a certain degree of transparency.
Although it is not necessary to disclose all technical details, the basic logic must be explained.
For example, a recommendation system provides suggestions based on the user's browsing history.
This way, users can understand why they see certain content.
If a system makes an important decision, such as automatically rejecting an application, users should know the main reason and have a chance to appeal.
The source of training data is also important.
Companies should ensure that data is obtained lawfully and does not contain sensitive information, such as health records or ID numbers.
Regularly checking data quality can reduce erroneous results.
Employees need to receive training, understand the importance of privacy protection, and know the consequences of violating the rules.
Finally, enterprises must formulate clear policies and accept external oversight.
Third-party audits can help discover vulnerabilities.
Publishing an annual transparency report can make the public trust the service more.
Overall, disclosing data practices and algorithm principles is not a burden, but a key step in building long-term trust.

People yawn when they are tired.
When yawning, the mouth opens very wide and takes in a lot of air.
This is a function of the body.
Scientists study this phenomenon, and this is called biology.
Yawning may be related to the temperature of the brain.
When the brain is too hot, yawning can make it a little cooler.
Neurology is the science that studies the brain and nerves.
Neurology has found that when people see others yawn, they also want to yawn.
This is the contagiousness of yawning.
When you see a classmate yawn in the classroom, you may also want to yawn right away.
Animals do this too.
Yawning is not because of laziness; it is because the body needs it.
We should listen to our bodies.
When sleepy, yawn, and then go to sleep.
